Indigo Plateau Sim

Can this team beat the Elite Four? Thousands of simulated runs, played by the games' own battle code.

v0.2 · FireRed: compiled pret/pokefirered · Crystal: ported pret/pokecrystal

FireRed's own battle engine, compiled from pret/pokefirered to WebAssembly and run in your browser. Enemy teams, AI, items and damage math are the game's code, not a re-implementation. Your side is played by a search that tries every option against the same simulated luck and keeps the best one. It knows the enemy teams and AI, but not future random rolls.

Your team

      Moves and levels are checked against Generation 3 (Ruby, Sapphire, Emerald, FireRed and LeafGreen); anything that isn't legal is marked, and you can still run it. Leave a Pokémon blank to run with fewer than six. The dice next to a Pokémon rerolls just that one (or fills an empty slot). Open "Nature, EVs, IVs" under a Pokémon to set its stats; EVs above 510 in total aren't possible in the game but are allowed here.

            Your Pokémon

            These runs used the game's own AI, which never switches. It sends Pokémon out in team order, so here wins added mostly measures who leads. A negative number means the team did better without that Pokémon in its slot. Use Search for a fairer read.

            KOs and faints come from the runs above. Wins added reruns the same runs, with the same luck, once without each Pokémon, and reports how many points the clear rate drops. It costs about as much as the original batch per Pokémon. All Pokémon are measured together, so every row fills in as it goes; the ± shrinks as runs come in, and you can stop once the numbers settle. Two Pokémon that do the same job each look less valuable, because the other one covers for it.

            Game plan

            Turns the runs above into a few rules you can follow in your own game: what to click in each matchup and who to send in after a faint. Each candidate plan is played on hundreds to thousands of fresh runs, and the most reliable plan with the fewest rules wins. Takes a few minutes (a single fight is quicker); keep this tab in view, since browsers slow down background tabs.

                    Checked against the real ROM

                    What's modeled and what isn't

                    The game's own code

                    • Battle engine, battle scripts and damage formula, compiled from pret/pokefirered
                    • Trainer AI scripts, AI switching and Full Restore use
                    • Enemy teams, natures and IVs as the game builds them
                    • Your bag items applied by the same code the bag menu calls, including in-battle heals and X items
                    • Exp and level-ups between fights (new moves are declined)

                    Assumptions

                    • All 8 badges. Battle style is your choice: Set (the game's option where you aren't offered a switch when the foe's Pokémon faints) or Shift (you are, and taking the offer is one of the player's options). Hardcore nuzlocke rules use Set. Shift battles aren't part of the ROM check yet.
                    • Choose the lead: before each fight the player may put any healthy Pokémon first, as you can in the party menu. It tries each one with quick playouts of the fight and keeps the best for the goal. The game's own AI keeps your order.
                    • One EV, IV and nature setting for every Pokémon
                    • Double battles and Shift style prompts aren't used
                    • The real game advances the random number generator every frame. Here it's reseeded at each of your decisions, which matches the ROM exactly when replayed but doesn't reproduce frame timing.
                    • Between fights the search compares five healing plans by simulating the next fight with the game's AI playing your side. The healing choice aims to win the next fight; it doesn't follow the goal setting.
                    • Only your actual decisions follow the goal. Inside each look-ahead playout, a quick stand-in player just tries to win. So a goal like Win fast picks the fastest option at each turn, but it won't discover a long setup plan by itself.
                    • With Search, each run is replayed with the same rolls by a reference player that can see them coming, which is how the luck breakdown is measured. That replay is cheap next to the search itself.
                    • Quick (128 playouts) uses a small trained model to skip the options it judges clearly worse, so all its playouts go to the 3 most promising moves or switches. On the 12-boss benchmark (hardcore rules, Win without losses, 480 battles, same luck) Quick won 58% of fights with it vs 49% without (+9 points). With 256 or more playouts it made no measurable difference, so Standard and Deep don't use it. The model was trained on the search's own choices in 3,000 battles with random teams, none of them the benchmark's. The model in use is standin-v1 (trained 2026-09-25).
                    • Quick's trained model tended to drop setup moves (Swords Dance, Dragon Dance...): in battles the full search played, its top 3 left out the setup move the search picked 36-46% of the time. Quick now always keeps them. In test fights built so that setting up is what wins (100 each, same luck), that raised Quick from 55% to 68% (Kingler vs Blaine) and from 93% to 100% (Scyther vs Koga), level with Standard; on the 12-boss benchmark it made no measurable difference (-0.4 points, 480 battles).
                    • Quick used to be 64 playouts. A faster battle engine (same battles, about twice the speed) let it double to 128 at about the same wait, which raised it from 47% to 58% of fights won (+10 points, same test as above).
                    • Game plan: on the 12-boss benchmark, plans of 1 to 5 rules won 65.8% on average on 10,000 fresh runs per boss, against 61.3% for the search re-thinking every turn and 37.4% for the game's own AI. A fixed plan can't lean on a lucky roll, so the most reliable plans favor moves that stop the opponent from acting (sleep, paralysis, a sure KO) and the right switch at the right time.
                    • One fight covers every gym leader, rival battle and Giovanni fight, using the game's own trainer data. The level cap is that trainer's highest level.
                    • Win by a thread scores each won fight by what was left at the end: fewer Pokémon standing first, then less HP on them. In a full run, each fight is scored on its own, so the player aims for a tight finish every fight, even though that leaves it weaker for the next one. A win still always beats a loss.
                    • Sweeps and KOs are credited to whichever of your Pokémon was in battle that turn, so poison or recoil KOs count for it too.
                    • Hardcore nuzlocke: no items, every Pokémon capped at the highest level on the other side (the Champion's, for a full run), and a Pokémon that faints stays out. The search then scores a win with fewer faints above a win with more.
                    • Player strength, on a 12-boss benchmark with the same luck for every player: the game's own AI playing your side wins 39%, the search at 256 playouts 62%, at 1,024 about 70%, and a search that knows every future roll 82%. In a hardcore-rules, Win-without-losses test: Quick (128) won 58%, 256 playouts 62% and Standard (512) 65%.
                    • Standard used to be 256 playouts. A faster battle engine (same battles, about twice the speed) let it double to 512 at about the same wait. On two independent sets of 480 battles (hardcore rules, Win without losses, same luck) it won about 6 points more (+3 and +10) and lost fewer Pokémon per win (1.23 to 1.05, and 1.21 to 1.13).
                    • Goals, on the same benchmark at 256 playouts: Win without losses raises wins with no faints from 4% to 13% with no measurable change in overall wins. Win fast wins about 0.8 turns sooner per fight (roughly 6%) at the same win rate.
                    • At the old Quick look-ahead of 64 playouts (480 battles each, same luck): Win with fewest Pokémon sends out about 0.2 fewer Pokémon per won fight (roughly 7%) at the same win rate. Shift style showed no measurable change in wins (+4 points, within noise).
                    • Choosing the lead (hardcore rules, Win without losses, 480 battles each with the team in a random order, same luck): at 256 playouts the player won 59% with it on vs 53% keeping the typed order (+7 points, a real difference); at Quick +4 points (within noise). If your first Pokémon is already a good lead, it makes no measurable difference.
                    • Win by a thread, same test: fights won with one Pokémon left standing rise from 45% to 86% of wins, and the average leftover drops from 1.4 to 0.6 Pokémon's worth. The cost is about 6 points of wins (±5).

                      What this MVP models, and what it doesn't

                      Ported from the disassembly

                      • Damage formula, 217–255 roll, crits with stage-ignoring rule, 1-byte stat truncation
                      • Type chart applied row by row in ROM order (it floors after each row)
                      • Johto badge stat boosts, including the Glacier Badge Sp. Def bug, and badge type boosts
                      • Trainer DVs, E4 movesets, and AI layers: Basic, Setup, Smart, Aggressive, Cautious, Status, Risky
                      • AI heal-item logic (highest-level mon only) and the 25% AI status-move fail
                      • Enemy replacement choice (FindMonInOTPartyToSwitchIntoBattle)

                      Simplified or missing

                      • Your side plays a greedy policy: highest expected damage, no voluntary switching, no in-battle items
                      • Enemy never switches voluntarily; Baton Pass fails
                      • No held items on your team
                      • Independent random draws, not the Game Boy's frame-timed RNG
                      • No differential test against the ROM yet

                      Plain-language explanations of the terms used on this page: what the numbers mean, the Pokémon rules involved, and how the simulator plays and checks battles.

                      The results on the pageGoals: what the player tries to doPokémon termsHow the engine worksHow the player is modeled

                      The results on the page

                      Clear rate
                      The share of simulated runs that beat every fight you asked for. In Full run mode that means all four Elite Four members and the Champion in a row, with no healing except what your bag allows. In One fight mode it's the win rate against that one trainer. 40% means 40 of every 100 simulated attempts made it to the end.
                      Deathless clear
                      The share of runs that cleared without a single one of your Pokémon fainting. This is the headline number in Hardcore nuzlocke mode, because in a nuzlocke a faint is permanent: a win that costs your starter is not a good outcome.
                      Faints per run
                      The average number of your Pokémon that were knocked out by the end of a run (win or loss).
                      ± pts (95%)
                      How much the headline number could move just from simulation noise. "48% ± 6 pts" means that if you ran the whole batch again, you'd expect to land between about 42% and 54% most of the time. More runs make this range smaller.
                      Funnel (Beat Lorelei, Beat Bruno…)
                      What share of runs got past each fight. It shows where a team's run usually ends. A big drop at one trainer means that fight is the wall.
                      Sample run
                      One complete simulated run, replayed with the battle text turned on so you can read exactly what happened. You can view a winning or a losing run from the same batch. Pick "Every run, one by one" or press ‹ › (or the ← → keys in that panel) to step through every run of the batch; with Watch open, the viewer follows along.
                      Debug info
                      A button in the Sample run panel that copies a small report: the exact run the panel is showing (your team, the opponent, the luck number, the look-ahead, goal, rules and bag), the version of the page, and where the replay is. Paste it to whoever is debugging: it replays that exact battle, move for move, with the same numbers the page showed.
                      Showdown log
                      The same sample run written in the text format Pokémon Showdown uses for replays (lines like |move| and |-damage|), one log per fight, because a Showdown log holds one battle. It's there so the battles can be played back in a replay viewer, such as the cartridge-replay project. It only contains Showdown's own line types: the viewer writes the battle text itself, so game-only text (EXP, prize money, trainer lines) is left out. HP is exact (like 150/217) rather than a percentage, and an item used from the bag appears as the Pokémon's heal or boost "from" that item.
                      Watch
                      Plays the sample run's fight in the cartridge-replay viewer, in the Sample run panel: the battle drawn with Pokémon Emerald's own sprites, text and animations, from the fight's Showdown log. With the Showdown log shown, it plays the fight you picked; otherwise the run's last fight. The viewer loads from acko.cool/replay when you first press Watch, so it needs an internet connection; nothing is sent there, the log stays in your browser. Click inside the replay to turn its sound on.
                      Win chance gauge (experimental)
                      Shown beside Watch: an estimate, at every decision of the fight, of the chance to win from that moment with strong play (and, dashed, to win with no Pokémon fainting). It comes from a small model trained on 20,000 simulated battles with playthrough-style teams, which looks only at the position (Pokémon left, HP, status, stat changes, speed, how hard each side hits); it doesn't simulate anything. It answers "how does the simulator's player usually do from here", so a newer player would do worse than it says, and it can be off by 5-10 points. Below the chart: Key decisions and Luck (runs played by the search only; game AI runs list the biggest swings instead).
                      Options this turn
                      In its own panel under the replay, for the moment the replay is at: every option the player (the search) considered, in the order it ranked them (it tries every option, drops the weaker half, and repeats, so options that lasted longer got more tries), with each option's share of its imagined battles won and won with no faints, and how many it tried. The pick is starred. "Clear choice" means the pick beat every other option by more than the look-ahead's own noise (on the same luck); "close call" means at least one other option was about as good, so either could be right. Options that fell behind early get fewer tries, so their numbers are rougher, and all of them run low (the imagined battles are finished by a simple stand-in player), so read them as a comparison. Quick skips some options before simulating; the list says how many.
                      Equally good / Inaccuracy / Mistake / Blunder
                      Move grades in Options this turn. The player's look-ahead compares each option with its pick on the same luck. "Equally good" options are ones it can't tell apart from its pick (the gap is within its own noise, or under 2 points of your goal's score); they're listed with stronger attacks first (super-effective before not very effective), then other moves, switches and items, because which of them the player actually played is a coin flip. The rest are graded by how much of the goal's score they give up: Inaccuracy under 5 points, Mistake under 15, Blunder above, with the noise shown (±). A decision with many options gives each fewer tries, so more of them come out "equally good". "Does nothing" marks a move that certainly fails by the game's rules (the foe is immune to it, already has that status or confusion, or is already seeded); it's never counted as equally good, even when the imagined battles can't tell the difference.
                      Key decisions
                      Moments in the Watch fight where the player's choice clearly beat every alternative, with each option's chance to win (or to win with no faints). The numbers come from the player's own look-ahead: before choosing, it plays each option out many times on the same luck, so the gap measures the choice and not the dice. A moment is listed only if the pick beat each alternative by at least 10 points and by more than the look-ahead's own noise. Most turns aren't listed because the options were close. The numbers run low: the look-ahead finishes each simulated battle with a simple stand-in player, which plays worse than the search, so read them as a comparison between options.
                      Luck (and the foe's play)
                      Moments in the Watch fight where what happened moved the odds furthest from what the chosen option was expected to give: a crit, a miss, a status, a damage roll, or the foe's own choice. Measured with the same look-ahead as Key decisions: the chosen option's chance before, and the best option's chance at the next decision. Listed from 15 points up.
                      Items left on average
                      How many bag items were still unused at the end of a run. A low number means the team needed its items to get through.
                      Turns per run
                      Battle turns across all the fights in a run, win or lose. It's the Win fast goal's measure of speed; it doesn't count text or animation time.
                      Sweep
                      A won fight where every enemy Pokémon was knocked out while the same one of your Pokémon was in battle. KOs from poison, recoil and similar count for whoever was in battle that turn.
                      Closest call / Safest win
                      For each run, the page tracks the lowest your team's total HP got (all six Pokémon added together). The safest win is the winning run where that low point was highest; the closest call is the winning run where it was lowest.
                      Luck breakdown
                      Each run is replayed with exactly the same rolls by a reference player that can see those rolls coming. Runs it also fails were lost to luck this team couldn't play around. Runs it clears but the normal player didn't were winnable in hindsight.
                      Winnable in hindsight
                      A failed run where a player who knew the upcoming rolls cleared it. It means a different choice would have worked with that luck. It doesn't mean the normal player made a mistake: it couldn't see the rolls.
                      KOs per run
                      How many enemy Pokémon were knocked out, on average per run, while this Pokémon was in battle.
                      Wins added
                      How many points the clear rate drops when this Pokémon is left out, measured by replaying the same runs with the same luck on a five-Pokémon team. It's a leave-one-out version of baseball's WAR (wins above replacement), with an empty slot as the replacement. Two Pokémon that do the same job can each look small, because the other covers for it.
                      Gauge only
                      Shows the odds without the battle logs or the team breakdown, so it tells you how likely you are to win a fight without showing how to win it. Meant for nuzlocke runs where seeing the solution would spoil the challenge.
                      Pokémon used
                      How many different Pokémon from your team were sent into battle during a run, counting the lead. The Win with fewest Pokémon goal puts a price on each one, so the player prefers winning with a smaller part of the team.
                      Choose the lead
                      Before each fight, the player may put any healthy Pokémon in front, as you can in the party menu between fights. The search tries each possible lead with quick playouts of the fight on the same luck and keeps the one that scores best for the goal. The game's own AI keeps your order.
                      Last one standing (sample run)
                      A choice in the sample-run picker: the winning run whose tightest fight ended closest to one Pokémon left on a sliver of HP. It uses the same measure as the Win by a thread goal, but you can pick it under any goal.
                      Game plan
                      A short list of rules you can follow in your own game: what to use or switch to in a given matchup (sometimes only at a certain HP bar color or status), who to send in after a faint, and which items to use between fights. The page builds it from the runs above: every situation the player met becomes a candidate rule, each candidate plan is played on hundreds to thousands of fresh runs, and rules are added one at a time (or in pairs) only while they clearly raise the success rate. Rules that don't pay for themselves are dropped, so the plan stays easy to remember. The headline number comes from 4,000 fresh runs the plan was never tuned on. Anything no rule covers falls back to: use your strongest move; after a faint, send in the next Pokémon (or whoever can hit hardest, whichever works better). Your team order is kept, so the first Pokémon leads. The luck in the simulator is typical luck, not your cartridge's exact random numbers, so the plan tells you what works most often, not a move-for-move script.

                      Goals: what the player tries to do

                      Goal
                      What your side is trying to achieve. The search tries each option many times and picks the one whose outcomes score best, and the goal decides how an outcome is scored. Rules are separate: they set the constraints (items, level cap, permanent faints, battle style), and the goal sets how the player plays within them. The line above the results always says the current goal in plain words. The game's own AI player ignores the goal: it plays its usual way whatever you pick.
                      How outcomes are scored
                      Every simulated fight ends with a score between 0 and about 1. A win starts near 1 (a little more with more HP left), and a loss scores near 0 (a little more if you did damage first). Each goal then subtracts a price for the things it wants to avoid. Prices are charged on wins (faints are also charged on look-ahead playouts that get cut off before the fight ends), so a goal never makes losing more attractive.
                      Exchange rates
                      The prices a goal charges, written as points of win chance. "A faint costs 30 points" means the player will accept a plan that wins 30 percentage points less often if it avoids one faint. You can see and change them under Exchange rates below the Goal menu. Changing any slider turns the goal into "Custom", and you can combine prices: for example, avoid faints and finish fast at the same time.
                      A win always beats a loss
                      However many faints, turns or Pokémon a win costs, it still scores above every loss (a win never drops below 0.32; a loss tops out at 0.30). So no goal will ever throw a fight on purpose. Goals only change which way of winning the player prefers, and how much win chance it will give up for it.
                      Win
                      The default. Maximize the chance of winning. When two options are about equally likely to win, the one that leaves more HP breaks the tie. In a full run, HP left over and unused bag items also count, because they help in the fights still to come. Exchange rates: none. This is the player all the benchmark numbers are based on.
                      Win without losses
                      For nuzlockes, where a fainted Pokémon is gone for good. Each faint during a fight costs 30 points of win chance, so a plan that wins 70% of the time with no faints beats one that wins 90% of the time with one faint. It's the default when you pick Hardcore nuzlocke rules, but you can use it with any rules. Measured effect: wins with no faints went from 4% to 13% on the benchmark, with no measurable change in overall wins.
                      Win fast
                      For speedruns. Each turn of a fight costs 1 point of win chance (0 to 3 with the slider), counted from the start of that fight. It prefers the quicker of two similar wins, but it won't gamble a win away to save a turn or two. Turns are battle turns, not real-time text or animation time. Measured effect: about 0.8 fewer turns per fight won (roughly 6% faster) at the same win rate.
                      Win with fewest Pokémon
                      Win while sending as few different Pokémon into battle as possible. Each Pokémon that enters a fight costs 10 points of win chance, and the lead counts. In a full run it counts different Pokémon across the whole run, so bringing back one you already used costs nothing extra. It pairs naturally with Choose the lead. Measured effect: about 0.2 fewer Pokémon per fight won (roughly 7%) at the same win rate.
                      Win by a thread
                      Just for fun: win with as little to spare as possible. Each fight you win is scored by what's left at the end: Pokémon still standing beyond the last one, plus the share of HP left on them. One Pokémon on 5% HP scores 0.05; two at full HP score 2. Each point of that costs 12 points of win chance, so the ideal finish is one Pokémon on a sliver of HP. In a full run every fight is scored on its own, even though a tight finish leaves you weaker for the next one. Measured effect: wins ending with one Pokémon standing went from 45% to 86% of wins, at a cost of about 6 points of wins.
                      Why there's no "Win safely"
                      A goal that judged each option by its worst luck, not its average, was built and tested. At half strength it made no measurable difference, and at full strength it cost 28 points of wins. The worst quarter of simulated outcomes is usually all losses, so it ended up ranking options by how much damage you deal while losing. To see how much a team depends on luck, use the Luck breakdown in the results.
                      Which decisions follow the goal
                      Every real choice in battle follows the goal: moves, switches, items, the Shift offer, and the lead when Choose the lead is on. Two things don't. First, inside each look-ahead playout a quick stand-in player just tries to win, so the search picks the best next step for the goal but won't plan a long, goal-specific sequence by itself; that's why the measured effects above are modest. Second, healing between fights picks the plan that best wins the next fight, whatever the goal.

                      Pokémon terms

                      Elite Four / Champion
                      The final gauntlet at Indigo Plateau: four trainers (Lorelei, Bruno, Agatha, Lance) and then the Champion, your rival. You fight them back to back without visiting a Pokémon Center.
                      First run / Rematch
                      In FireRed and LeafGreen the Elite Four's teams get stronger after you finish the post-game islands. First run is the version you meet the first time through.
                      Your starter
                      The rival picks the starter that beats yours, so your choice decides which Champion team you face (for example, pick Charmander and the rival has Blastoise).
                      Nuzlocke
                      A self-imposed challenge ruleset. The core rules: you may only catch the first Pokémon you meet in each area, and a Pokémon that faints is treated as dead and can't be used again.
                      Hardcore nuzlocke
                      A stricter nuzlocke. On this page it means: no items, a level cap, and faints are permanent. The simulator scores wins with fewer faints above wins with more.
                      Level cap
                      A hardcore nuzlocke rule: none of your Pokémon may be above the highest level on the opponent's team. For a full Elite Four run the cap is the Champion's highest level. The page lowers any Pokémon above the cap to the cap.
                      Imported opponent team
                      In One fight you can give the opponent a different team: paste a pokepast.es link or Showdown's export format under the opponent. Only the Pokémon change: the trainer keeps their own AI, bag items and name, so it's that trainer's game logic playing the team (for example Lance's AI and Full Restores with a custom team). Anything Generation 3 doesn't have is rejected, moves or levels that aren't legal in Gen 3 are marked but still run, and the nuzlocke level cap becomes the imported team's highest level. "Use their own team" goes back to the trainer's real party.
                      Boss
                      A fight that matters for tracking progress: a gym leader, an Elite Four member, the Champion, or Giovanni.
                      EVs (effort values)
                      Hidden points a Pokémon earns from battles that raise its stats a little. Each stat can get up to 255, with a total cap of 510 in these games. On the FireRed tab you set them per Pokémon under "Nature, EVs, IVs" (a new slot starts at 40 in every stat, like a light playthrough); totals above 510 are allowed there but can't happen in the game.
                      IVs (individual values)
                      A Pokémon's hidden genetic stat bonuses, 0 to 31 per stat, fixed when it's caught. Higher is better. On the FireRed tab you set them per Pokémon (a new slot starts at 20). In Generation 3 they also decide Hidden Power's type.
                      DVs and stat exp (Crystal)
                      The Generation 2 versions of IVs and EVs. DVs run 0 to 15; stat exp runs up to 65,535 per stat. They only matter on the Crystal tab.
                      Nature
                      In Generation 3, each Pokémon has a nature that raises one stat by 10% and lowers another by 10%. Five natures (Hardy, Docile, Serious, Bashful, Quirky) change nothing; those are marked neutral.
                      Happiness (friendship)
                      A hidden 0 to 255 value that sets the power of Return (stronger when high) and Frustration (stronger when low). Left blank, a Pokémon has its species' normal starting value, as when first caught. An imported paste uses its Happiness line, or 255 (0 with Frustration), as Pokémon Showdown does.
                      Legal (Gen 3)
                      Whether a Pokémon could really know its moves at its level in Generation 3: Ruby, Sapphire, Emerald, FireRed or LeafGreen, since Pokémon can be traded between them (the rule Pokémon Showdown's ADV formats use). A move counts if the Pokémon or an earlier evolution learns it by level-up at or below its level, by TM or HM, from a move tutor, as an egg move, or from an official event. A Pokémon also can't be below the level it evolves at (no level 30 Charizard). Anything that isn't legal is marked in the team and listed below it, with the reason, but the simulation still runs, so 'what if' teams work. Combinations that can't happen together (two egg moves from incompatible parents, say) aren't checked.
                      Pokepaste import
                      Load your team from a pokepast.es link or from text in Pokémon Showdown's team-export format. The import is strict: a paste with anything FireRed doesn't have (a later Pokémon, move, item or ability, Tera Types, more than 510 EVs, Hidden Power IVs that don't match its type) is rejected with the reasons listed, rather than changed. Moves or levels that exist in Gen 3 but aren't legal for that Pokémon are imported and marked, like in the editor (see Legal). Nicknames, gender and shininess aren't used, and your opponent's team still comes from the game.
                      Randomize team
                      Fills all six slots with a random Gen 3 Pokémon (any of the 386 that can legally be that level, no repeats) at your opponent's top level (the champion's for a full Elite Four run). Its moves are ones it can learn in Gen 3 by that level, by TM or HM, from a tutor or as an egg move (from Pokémon Showdown's data; event-only moves are left out), picked so it has at least two attacking moves, one of its own type when it can, and never two attacks of the same type. Ability, nature, held item, EVs (a legal spread, 510 at most) and IVs are random too.
                      Random mode: Fair, Smart, Full
                      How Randomize team and the dice pick Pokémon. Fair (playthrough), the default: only Pokémon a FireRed player could have by the chosen fight (the Elite Four for a full run): caught in the areas reachable by then or received as gifts, with your starter; evolved by level, by stone once stones can be bought, never by trade; the moves they'd know by level-up plus TMs and HMs you'd have; levels uneven around the cap, like a real run. Against Brock that means your starter and Route 1, Route 22, Route 2 and Viridian Forest Pokémon, not Alakazam. Smart: any of the 386 at the level cap with sensible moves (at least two attacks, one of its own type when it can). Full: any of the 386 with any four moves it can learn in Gen 3. The story order behind Fair is hand-written from FireRed's progression, so it's a close approximation.
                      Randomize one Pokémon (the dice)
                      The dice next to a Pokémon rerolls just that one, the same way Randomize team picks each Pokémon (at your opponent's top level, with moves it can learn in Gen 3), and never picks a species already on your team. On an empty slot it adds a random Pokémon.
                      Ability
                      A passive trait each Pokémon has (for example Intimidate lowers the foe's Attack on entry). Some species can have one of two abilities; the page lets you pick.
                      Held item
                      An item a Pokémon carries into battle that works on its own, such as Leftovers (restores a little HP each turn) or a Sitrus Berry (heals once when HP gets low).
                      Bag items
                      Items you use from the menu during or between battles, like Full Restore or Revive. Using one in battle costs your turn.
                      Badges
                      Gym badges also give small stat boosts in battle. The simulator assumes you have all eight, as you would at the Elite Four.
                      Battle style: Set vs Shift
                      A game option. With Shift (the game's default), when the foe's Pokémon faints you're told what it will send next and asked whether you want to switch first: a free switch. With Set you're not asked. The page lets you choose; the Shift offer becomes one of the player's decisions. Hardcore nuzlocke rules use Set.
                      RNG (random number generator)
                      The game's source of luck: damage rolls, critical hits, misses, how long sleep lasts, whether a status effect triggers. Battles with the same choices can go very differently because of it.

                      How the engine works

                      Decomp (decompilation)
                      A community project that rebuilt the game's original C source code from the cartridge. pret/pokefirered and pret/pokecrystal are decomps: when compiled, they produce a ROM identical to the retail game, byte for byte.
                      pret
                      The community group that maintains the Pokémon decomps on GitHub.
                      ROM
                      The game's program and data as one file, what's on the cartridge.
                      Compiling
                      Turning source code into a program a machine can run. Here the FireRed battle code is compiled twice: once for the Game Boy Advance (to check against the real game) and once for your browser.
                      WebAssembly (WASM)
                      A format that lets compiled programs run inside a web browser at near-native speed. The FireRed tab runs the game's actual battle code this way, rather than a rewrite of it.
                      Stubs
                      Stand-in pieces of code that do nothing. The battle code expects graphics, sound and menus to exist; in the browser those are replaced with stubs, so only the battle logic runs.
                      Hand port (Crystal tab)
                      The Crystal engine was rewritten by hand in JavaScript from the decomp, so it can contain transcription mistakes. That's why it's labeled as the older, less verified version.
                      Emulator / mGBA
                      An emulator is a program that pretends to be a game console so a ROM can run on a computer. mGBA is a widely used, accurate Game Boy Advance emulator.
                      Differential test
                      Running the same battle two ways and checking they agree. Here: play a battle in the browser engine, record every choice and random seed, replay those exact choices in the real FireRed ROM under mGBA, and compare HP, status and active Pokémon at every decision.
                      Harness (test harness)
                      A small modified build of the game that plays a scripted battle automatically and writes down what happened, so the comparison can run without anyone holding a controller.
                      State mismatch
                      Any point where the browser engine and the real ROM disagree about the battle (different HP, status, active Pokémon or turn). The published checks found none.
                      Seed / reseeding
                      A seed is a starting number that decides what the random number generator produces. The real game changes its random numbers every frame; the simulator instead sets a fresh seed at each of your decisions. That makes battles reproducible and lets the ROM check match exactly.
                      Snapshot
                      A saved copy of the entire battle state. The search takes one before trying an option and restores it afterward, like a save state in an emulator. It takes about a tenth of a millisecond.

                      How the player is modeled

                      Monte Carlo simulation
                      Answering a question by simulating it many times and counting outcomes, instead of solving it exactly. "This team clears 40% of the time" comes from running the full gauntlet hundreds of times with different luck.
                      Run
                      One complete simulated attempt: every fight in the selected set, played start to finish.
                      Player model
                      Whatever decides your side's moves, switches and items in the simulation. All the numbers depend on how good it is: a weak player model makes teams look worse than they are.
                      The game's own trainer AI
                      The same decision code the Elite Four uses, borrowed to play your side. It's fast and reasonable but never switches out, so it's the baseline the search is measured against.
                      Search
                      The stronger player model. At each of your decisions it tries every legal option (each move, switch and item), plays the rest of the battle out many times, and picks the option that did best.
                      Playout (rollout)
                      One simulated continuation of the battle to the end, used to judge an option. Inside a playout a quick stand-in player makes the moves.
                      Stand-in player
                      The fast rule-based player used inside playouts. The one used on the page attacks with its best expected-damage move but switches out of a losing matchup when a teammate takes the hit much better.
                      Look-ahead / budget (playouts per decision)
                      How many playouts the search spends on each decision. Quick is 128, Standard 512, Deep 1024. More is stronger but slower; on the benchmark the search wins about 62% at 256 playouts vs the game AI's 39%, and 512 adds about 6 points.
                      Same-luck comparison (common random numbers)
                      Every option is tested against the same sampled luck, so one option doesn't look better just because it happened to get the good rolls. This mattered more than anything else for strength.
                      Successive halving
                      The search tests every option a little, drops the worse half, and spends the remaining playouts on the better half. It puts effort where the decision is actually close.
                      Tree search (MCTS)
                      A search that also plans your follow-up decisions, not just the next one. It was tested and lost to the simpler search at practical speeds, because splitting the playouts across more decisions made each estimate too noisy.
                      Knows-the-future reference (oracle)
                      A search allowed to see the upcoming random rolls. No real player can do that; it's used to show how much of a result is luck. On the benchmark it wins 82%.
                      Benchmark
                      A fixed set of 12 team-vs-boss battles used to measure player models. Every model plays the same battles with the same luck, so differences come from decisions, not dice.
                      Paired comparison
                      Comparing two player models battle by battle on identical luck, then averaging the differences. It detects real improvements with far fewer battles than comparing overall win rates.
                      Healing plan (between fights)
                      Before each Elite Four fight, the search compares a few ways of using bag items (none, revive only, patch up, top up, full heal) by simulating the next fight, and keeps the one that does best without wasting items.
                      Full info
                      The search knows every enemy team, moveset, item and the AI's rules, like a player reading a guide. It does not know future random rolls.
                      Quick's shortcut (learned pruning)
                      Before a Quick search simulates anything, a small trained model scores every move and switch and keeps only its top 3, so its 128 playouts aren't spread thin over options that are clearly worse. The model learned from the search itself: it watched the search play 3,000 battles with random teams against every boss and learned which options it tends to pick. It rarely drops a good option: in battles it never saw, its top 3 included one the search rated within 2 points of its best 92% of the time. It helps when playouts are scarce (+9 points at 128) and makes no measurable difference with more of them, so only Quick uses it. Setup moves (Swords Dance, Dragon Dance, Calm Mind...) are always kept: the model tended to drop them, and in fights where setting up is what wins, keeping them brought Quick level with Standard.

                      No terms match.
